analysis.one_liner: Shifted savings-and-loan bailout costs onto high earners, corporations, and the industry itself instead of borrowing, and expanded fraud enforcement.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 29 House members, was referred to three committees in August 1990 and never received a markup or a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The savings-and-loan cleanup had ballooned from an estimated $50 billion to as much as $132 billion, and the government was paying for it by borrowing, which the bill's findings said would push the true long-run cost past $1.3 trillion with interest. This bill would instead pay the bills as they came due: a 7.5% surtax on investment income of people making over $100,000, a 5% surtax on profitable corporations, an end to the tax break that lets heirs sell inherited assets without ever paying tax on the old gains, and new assessments on the thrift industry. It also gave regulators and private citizens more tools to go after savings-and-loan fraud.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers generally, especially those earning under $100,000, who would stop footing bailout costs through federal borrowing and interest payments; federal bank regulators, who would get injunction and asset-freezing powers in fraud cases; and private citizens, who could sue over financial-institution fraud and recover attorney fees if they prevailed.

how_it_helps.text: The bill's findings state that financing the rescue by borrowing would cost an estimated $456.3 billion by 1999 and $1.369 trillion by 2029 once all interest is paid, and that working-capital interest alone would add $28 billion by 1999; paying directly avoids most of that interest cost.

It imposes a 7.5% surtax on unearned income of individuals with adjusted gross income over $100,000 (phased in above that threshold) and a 5% surtax on corporate tax above $13,750, from 1990 through 1995, and deposits the money in a new trust fund for the Resolution Trust Corporation.

It replaces tax-free stepped-up basis on inherited appreciated property with carryover basis during the surtax period, so heirs pay tax on gains the deceased person never paid — with exemptions for a principal residence, farms, life insurance, and up to $10,000 in personal effects, and a $60,000 minimum-basis cushion.

It adds bank fraud and bribery crimes as racketeering offenses, lets regulators freeze defendants' assets before judgment in fraud cases, and lets private citizens sue fraudsters under the False Claims Act model with attorney fees if they win.

Its findings note that of roughly $16 billion in bailout costs attributed to criminal activity, less than $100 million had been recovered, and the FBI had taken no action on more than 21,000 referrals — the enforcement title is aimed at recovering more of that money.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals with incomes over $100,000 who have investment income, profitable corporations, estates and heirs of people dying after 1990 (who would lose tax-free treatment of inherited appreciation), and the thrift industry, which would face new assessments and mandatory payments from the Federal Home Loan Banks.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, corporations, heirs, thrift industry

drawbacks.text: The carryover basis rules would impose significant recordkeeping on executors, who must file information returns and give written basis notices to every recipient, with penalties up to $5,000 for failures — and heirs of appreciated family businesses could face tax bills on assets they inherit but do not sell.
The surtax period was set for 1990 through 1995, but the President could extend it year by year through 1998 if bailout financing fell short, so the tax could last longer than promised.

A corporate surtax raises the cost of doing business, and some of that cost can be passed to consumers through prices; the bill also concentrates bailout financing decisions in the Resolution Trust Corporation and Treasury.

Paying for the bailout up front through taxes means recognizing the full cost immediately in taxes rather than spreading it over decades, which critics of pay-as-you-go rescue funding argued burdened the current economy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade favors taxpayers as a whole: the bill's own findings show borrowing would roughly triple the long-run cost of the rescue through interest, so paying directly saves far more than the surtax raises in friction. The heaviest burdens fall on households above roughly $100,000, profitable corporations, and heirs of large estates — not on typical workers, who would see no surtax at all. The real design weak spots are the complexity of the carryover basis rules and the possibility the temporary tax gets extended; both are real but secondary to the central fiscal question of who pays for the rescue.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 1990, sent to three committees, and sent to two subcommittees — but no committee ever voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 3, 1990 by Representative Joseph P. Kennedy II with 28 cosponsors, all Democrats, and was referred jointly to the Committees on Ways and Means, Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs, and Judiciary.

In late August and early September 1990 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and the Banking Subcommittee on Financial Institutions Supervision, Regulation and Insurance — the last recorded action in its history.
No committee reported the bill, no chamber voted on it, and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 with the bill still parked in committee.
The urgency was real: the bill's findings record that the Administration raised its bailout cost estimate from $50 billion in August 1989 to between $90 billion and $132 billion by May 1990.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, households earning over $100,000, profitable corporations, and heirs of large estates avoided new taxes, and the thrift industry avoided new assessments — leaving the bailout financed by federal borrowing whose interest costs fall on future taxpayers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners, corporations, heirs, thrift industry

for.name: Joseph P. Kennedy II
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 28 cosponsors.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill's tax provisions on August 3, 1990 and never held a markup on them before the Congress ended.

against.name: House committee leadership (Banking and Judiciary)
against.role: Chairs of the two other committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Their committees and subcommittees took referrals of the bill through September 4, 1990, and no further action was ever recorded.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and no roll-call vote was ever taken, so opposition was never recorded by party — the bill simply never moved.

industries.industry: Savings and loan industry (thrifts and Federal Home Loan Banks)
industries.note: The bill would require Federal Home Loan Banks to pay roughly $300 million a year toward resolution funding and would let the Resolution Trust Corporation assess Savings Association Insurance Fund members the way the FDIC assesses banks. Today those resolution costs are financed by borrowing whose interest the public repays.

A 7.5% surtax would fall only on unearned income of taxpayers with incomes over $100,000, and heirs would lose the stepped-up basis that lets inherited gains go untaxed. Ordinary taxpayers under the threshold pay nothing under the bill.
A 5% surtax would apply to corporate tax liability above $13,750 for 1990 through 1995, raising the tax bill of profitable companies during the rescue period.

The bill authorizes private civil actions against financial-institution fraud with recovery of costs and reasonable attorney fees for substantially prevailing plaintiffs, creating a new enforcement docket.
